summary:
Bali stands under Indonesia's national framework, and that framework is where the legal risk sits. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted anywhere in Indonesia, that provision reaches consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. Same-sex marriage remains unrecognised for visitors and residents alike.

The island's own environment is materially milder than the statute book. Travel guidance current to March 2026 describes a "live and let live" basis, records no criminal enforcement against foreign tourists, and names Seminyak (Eat Street and Batu Belig), Canggu and Ubud as the areas with the most consistently LGBTQ+-friendly venues. Public displays of affection warrant discretion. A separate traveller-facing guide rates Bali 6.3 out of 10 overall but only 2.0 for legal safety, warning that LGBTQ+ travellers face legal risk under Indonesian national law and advising visitors to keep affection quiet despite the island's tolerant reputation.

Peer-reviewed ethnography published in 2025 documents the transpuan (trans feminine) community in Bali across four case studies, describing lives marked by discrimination and misrecognition alongside informal resistance. The academic record confirms that Bali hosts a visible trans community living with real precarity.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller in Indonesia. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges and died in custody; his mother alleges police beat him, and Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
Physical risk is rising across Indonesia. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue nationally. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law. Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity directly, and in Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Bali has no equivalent provincial provision.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; the national broadcasting commission banned presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal in March 2016, and websites and apps carrying LGBTQ-related words have been blocked.
localsOnly:
Indonesian law recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option on documents. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, a process residents must complete domestically.

No national anti-discrimination statute covers sexual orientation or gender identity, so residents have no statutory recourse against discrimination or harassment on those grounds. Transpuan communities documented in Bali live with precarity and misrecognition while maintaining informal networks of resistance.

A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025, which would affect residents' everyday expression more than short-term visitors'.
outOfScopeNotes:
The March 2026 travel guidance states that same-sex relations are not a criminal offence in Bali under Indonesian national law, while the Gayborhood guide warns that same-sex relations are criminalised in Indonesia. These framings are not fully reconciled: the 2026 penal code criminalises extra-marital sex rather than same-sex sex as such, but because same-sex marriage is unrecognised the effect reaches consensual same-sex relations. Whether the provision has been enforced against visitors in Bali remains unresolved in the sources.

Whether the villa raid pattern of June 2025 has extended to Bali specifically is not sourced here. The status of the 2025 online-content bill after its discussion stage is unresolved.
